section_summary: This section documents Japan’s worsening financial position in late 1931, especially the depletion of gold reserves, restoration of the gold embargo, abandonment of the gold standard, budget deficits, proposed taxation, and renewed borrowing. Reports connect these problems to military operations in Manchuria, the Chinese boycott, declining Sino-Japanese trade, shipping losses, unemployment, and competition between Japanese and British textile producers. The section also covers a French judgment on Tokyo municipal bonds, Cabinet politics surrounding Adachi and Inouye, preliminary 1932–1933 budget estimates, and State Department reluctance to encourage American loans to Japan while its intentions in Manchuria remained unclear.

subfiles.title: Continuation of report on capital flight, exchange restrictions, and the Japanese budget
subfiles.about: The fragment describes measures to prevent gold exports and the difficulty of reconciling departmental demands with Finance Ministry budget reforms.
subfiles.summary: The Bank of Japan raised its discount rate and the Yokohama Specie Bank restricted dollar exchange and large remittances, a practical unofficial gold embargo; the Government struggled with its budget as departments opposed the Finance Minister's economies, and General Minami urged a more positive policy.

subfiles.title: Document file note on Japan’s financial condition
subfiles.from: Miller, Department of State, Far Eastern Division
subfiles.about: The note cross-references material on Japan’s budget-balancing difficulties and the growing effects of the Chinese boycott.
subfiles.summary: Filing note to file 793.94/3164: Japan's finances grow difficult from the budget problem and first visible effects of the Chinese boycott.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 263 on Mitsui gold purchases and the Cabinet crisis
subfiles.from: W. Cameron Forbes, U.S. Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The telegram reports allegations that Mitsui interests accumulated gold dollars and supported Adachi’s maneuvers to bring down the Cabinet before imposition of a gold embargo.
subfiles.summary: Telegram 263: reports say Mitsui bought up to $200 million in gold dollars and backed Adachi's campaign against the Cabinet; the new Cabinet's immediate gold embargo would profit buyers hugely; Adachi and three supporters resigned from the Minseito.

subfiles.title: Document file note on telegram no. 1074 from China
subfiles.about: The note identifies a telegram reporting Chinese opinion that Japan’s apparent victory might prove pyrrhic because of its financial weakness.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to China telegram 1074: Chinese belief that the financial costs of Japan's actions could negate its apparent victory.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 1074 on Chinese acceptance of the League resolution and Japan’s finances
subfiles.from: Perkins, for the Minister, U.S. Legation, Peiping
subfiles.about: The telegram relays a Reuters report explaining China’s acceptance of the League of Nations resolution and predicting severe financial consequences for Japan.
subfiles.summary: Telegram 1074: Chinese officials found the League resolution unsatisfactory but accepted it to show good faith, lacking readiness for war; observers consider Japan's victory pyrrhic, as military costs, lost China exports and permanently larger Manchurian forces may overwhelm its finances.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 24 on the City of Tokyo 1912 bond judgment
subfiles.from: Williamson S. Howell Jr., for the Chargé d’Affaires ad interim, U.S. Embassy, Paris
subfiles.about: The despatch reports a French appellate judgment concerning payment of the City of Tokyo five-percent 1912 bonds.
subfiles.summary: Despatch 24: the Dijon Appeal Court ruled December 1 on the City of Tokyo's 100-million-franc 1912 bond issue that holders may demand interest and principal in francs converted at the day's sterling rate.

subfiles.title: Department of State memorandum on Economic Notes from Tokyo
subfiles.from: Department of State, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: The memorandum summarizes a Military Attaché report on the economic effects of the anti-Japanese boycott.
subfiles.summary: Memo on the Tokyo Military Attaché's November 17 report: October statistics show the boycott works, declining China trade hurt Japanese shipping, and many Japanese businesspeople had to leave China.

subfiles.title: Economic Notes, Tokyo Military Attaché Report no. 5971
subfiles.from: Thomas G. Cranford Jr., for the U.S. Military Attaché, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The report analyzes gold losses, debate over restoring the embargo, business conditions, China trade, cotton, shipping, returning businesspeople, and unemployment.
subfiles.summary: Report 5971: Japan's gold reserve fell sharply since the January 1930 embargo lifting, prompting exchange controls and pressure to restore the ban; the Manchurian Incident and boycott hit Osaka and Kobe, exports to China collapsed, ships sat idle, and official unemployment exceeded 400,000, perhaps over a million.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 406 on possible reimposition of the gold embargo
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, for the Ambassador, U.S. Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The despatch assesses growing support for restoring Japan’s gold-export embargo and the Government’s determination to maintain free gold exports.
subfiles.summary: Japan’s specie reserve had fallen from about ¥1.072 billion when the gold ban was lifted in January 1930 to ¥527.716 million on December 1, 1931. British suspension of gold conversion, Japan’s looming budget deficit, military operations in Manchuria, the Chinese boycott, and public advocacy by the Seiyukai, newspapers, and Sanji Muto all strengthened support for an embargo. Neville nevertheless believed the Minseito government would maintain free gold exports unless further depletion or political change made reversal unavoidable. Finance Minister Inouye defended the policy in Osaka and argued that Japan could withstand the effects of the Manchurian crisis and sterling depreciation.

subfiles.title: Document file note on Japanese taxation and the budget deficit
subfiles.about: The note identifies a report on increased taxation, abandonment of the no-loan policy, and the Japanese budget deficit.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to report 404: Japan's government must raise taxes, resume borrowing and address a large budget deficit.

subfiles.title: Government Finances: The Budget
subfiles.about: The excerpt outlines proposed tax increases, enterprise bonds, and other borrowing needed to balance Japan’s next budget.
subfiles.summary: Minseito leaders concluded falling revenue made dropping the no-loan policy unavoidable, proposing higher income, inheritance, gasoline and customs taxes and telephone, road, earthquake and deficit bonds, with war bonds contemplated for Manchuria; the press doubted the shrinking domestic market could absorb them.

subfiles.title: Document file note on despatch no. 2473 from Great Britain
subfiles.about: The note cross-references a despatch and Times editorial on Japan’s abandonment of the gold standard and its financial consequences.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to despatch 2473 from Britain with a December 14 Times editorial on Japan's finances, restored gold embargo and leaving the gold standard.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 2473 on Japan’s abandonment of the gold standard
subfiles.from: Ray Atherton, for the Ambassador, U.S. Embassy, London
subfiles.about: The despatch forwards and comments on a Times editorial about Japan’s Cabinet change, gold embargo, and economic competition with Britain.
subfiles.summary: Atherton questions the editorial’s claim that the Cabinet crisis was unrelated to Manchuria, citing confidential Japanese diplomatic reports that the military had effectively gained control of the Government. Japan’s heavy gold losses, falling exports to China, closed Japanese cotton mills in the Yangtze Valley, and commercial difficulties in China made departure from gold increasingly likely. The despatch examines how Chinese boycott orders had revived British cotton production and how yen depreciation could erase those gains in China, India, Africa, and other markets. Japan also benefited from lower production costs, geographic proximity to Asian markets, and large stocks of raw cotton purchased before depreciation.

subfiles.title: “Changes in Japan”
subfiles.about: The editorial interprets Japan’s new ministry and abandonment of the gold standard as products of financial conflict rather than the Manchurian crisis.
subfiles.summary: The Times says the Wakatsuki Ministry fell mainly from Adachi's conflict with Finance Minister Inouye and bankers' and industrialists' opposition to free gold exports; Seiyukai's immediate embargo confirms the financial character; Takahashi preserves confidence but Inukai's minority government stays precarious, with little policy change toward China.

subfiles.title: Government Budget: Budget Expenditures, Fiscal Year 1932–1933
subfiles.from: Thomas G. Cranford Jr., for the U.S. Military Attaché, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The report supplies preliminary departmental expenditure estimates for Japan’s 1932–1933 fiscal year.
subfiles.summary: Preliminary 1932-1933 expenditures about 1.48 billion yen, including 1.2 million for the Geneva Disarmament Conference; revenue stays about 120 million short, so the Finance Ministry is revising; about 100 delegates and staff leave for Marseille December 14.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 441 on delayed budget commentary
subfiles.from: W. Cameron Forbes, U.S. Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Forbes explains why the Embassy cannot yet comment adequately on Japan’s preliminary 1932–1933 budget.
subfiles.summary: The preliminary budget of the Cabinet that resigned on December 11 had not been completed before its fall. The new Government had also not released its preliminary budget in sufficient detail. Forbes therefore postponed the Embassy’s analysis until January.

subfiles.title: Memorandum file note on possible Japanese loan inquiries
subfiles.from: Hornbeck, Department of State, Far Eastern Division
subfiles.about: The memorandum records rumors that Japan was exploring a loan and recommends against encouraging American financiers while Japanese intentions in Manchuria remained unsatisfactory.
subfiles.summary: Far Eastern Division finds it logical that Japan would sound out lenders, and advises American financiers get no encouragement to lend until Japan's Manchuria intentions are clearer.
